strengths: The paper studies a simple, inexpensive geometric statistic and evaluates its association with perplexity across several model families, sizes, layers, and text domains.
The presentation is generally clear, with explicit definitions, extensive visualizations, and useful hyperparameter details in the appendix.
The training intervention and analysis of within- versus between-cluster dispersion are potentially interesting starting points for studying representation geometry.
weaknesses: A central model-selection result is contradicted by the paper's own Table 3. Using the stated gap, within-domain plus domain-to-reference distance, the eight listed Qwen checkpoints have Spearman correlations of only about 0.43 for Euclidean distance and 0.11 for cosine distance with accuracy—not greater than 0.95 or a perfect ranking as claimed. The text also refers to nine checkpoints although only eight are listed. Euclidean gaps are additionally confounded by embedding scale.

The purported label-free accuracy prediction experiment first uses ground-truth labels to partition examples into correct and incorrect sets and then constructs mixtures with prescribed accuracies. This only shows an aggregate association after labels are known; it does not demonstrate estimating accuracy on a genuinely unlabeled set. Pairwise dispersion is a set-level statistic, so the claimed ability to sort individual examples by dispersion is also undefined by the proposed method.

The kNN-LM application never runs a kNN-LM or reports retrieval-augmented perplexity. It only observes that attention outputs have greater dispersion than feed-forward outputs and assumes that the more dispersed representation is the better retrieval key. Consequently, the advertised claim that dispersion selects the optimal kNN-LM layer is unsupported.

The main correlation analysis is observational and vulnerable to content, difficulty, and binning confounds. Correlations and p-values are computed after sorting by perplexity, aggregating examples into bins, and deliberately sampling across the perplexity range, without comparison to simple uncertainty or geometry baselines. Lower ground-truth perplexity also does not imply the lower predictive entropy asserted in the motivation.

Average pairwise cosine distance has a simple dependence on the norm of the mean normalized representation; maximizing it can be achieved by centering or even antipodal collapse and does not necessarily produce a rich or discriminative geometry. This degeneracy is neither analyzed nor compared against covariance rank, isotropy, effective dimension, or contrastive alternatives.

The causal training evidence is weak: only single runs and short training horizons with very high perplexities are reported, lambda is selected separately by validation, and there are no uncertainty estimates, compute-matched controls, downstream evaluations, or evidence that gains persist to convergence. The cross-domain objective primarily pushes domain means apart and therefore does not establish the broader claimed mechanism.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code URL is blank, several dataset and token-set construction choices are unspecified, and important experimental details and seeds are absent. Fine-tuning comparisons are also confounded by different training durations. These issues, together with the numerical contradiction and unvalidated applications, leave several central claims unsupported.

The paper is generally readable and attempts to turn its geometric observation into practical applications, including model selection, retrieval-layer selection, and an auxiliary training objective.

The appendices provide many additional correlation plots and some training and sampling details; the observed within-model association between perplexity bins and dispersion appears across multiple architectures and datasets.
The intervention experiments at least attempt to go beyond purely observational correlations, and the reported cross-domain perplexity improvements are potentially interesting.
weaknesses: The proposed statistic does not generally measure geometric 'breadth.' For unit-normalized vectors, the average pairwise cosine distance is exactly N/(N-1) times one minus the squared norm of their mean. It therefore primarily measures cancellation of the mean direction and can be maximized by degenerate configurations, such as two opposing collapsed clusters. This undermines the paper's central geometric interpretation and the push-away objective.

The principal correlation analysis is heavily confounded. Examples are sorted and binned by perplexity, after which a set-level pairwise statistic is computed within each bin. There is no control for lexical composition, token frequency, topic, output entropy, or other factors that can jointly affect perplexity and hidden-state mean direction. Correlations and p-values over constructed bins do not establish the claimed fundamental relationship.

The paper repeatedly frames the result as a relationship across models, but most plots show correlations across input bins within one model. Dispersion values are not consistently ordered by model quality across architectures or sizes, and no controlled cross-model analysis establishes that a model with greater dispersion generally has lower perplexity.

The downstream-accuracy experiment does not demonstrate label-free prediction in the stated deployment setting. It first uses ground-truth labels to partition examples into correct and incorrect groups and then constructs artificial mixtures with prescribed accuracy. This neither predicts the accuracy of a naturally occurring unlabeled set nor shows that individual errors can be detected or sorted using the set-level pairwise metric.

The model-selection evidence changes from contextual representations to a handcrafted metric over output-token embeddings, without establishing why the earlier phenomenon transfers. It uses manually selected domain-token lists and only a very small, confounded collection of checkpoints differing in scale, family, and fine-tuning. Euclidean output-embedding distances are also sensitive to arbitrary scaling. The text claims perfect ranking of nine checkpoints, whereas Table 3 lists eight.

The kNN-LM application is unsupported by the necessary experiment: Table 1 reports only dispersion and provides no kNN-LM retrieval accuracy or perplexity for the candidate sublayers. Consequently, the claim that maximum dispersion identifies the best retrieval representation is inferred from prior work rather than demonstrated here. The appendix is also inconsistent about whether each plotted point represents a chunk-level statistic or a distance computed across chunks.

The training results lack repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, matched hyperparameter selection, and comparisons with relevant contrastive or isotropy regularizers. The auxiliary weight is selected from eleven values while the baseline is singular, both settings are evaluated after only 500–1000 steps with very high perplexities, and the paper does not verify that gains persist at convergence. It also does not report the resulting dispersion alongside performance.

Several causal or mechanistic statements are stronger than the evidence. Fine-tuning checkpoints simultaneously change loss and geometry; repeated 10-gram continuations are not necessarily semantically similar contexts; and the proposed cross-domain loss merely encourages opposing domain means rather than demonstrated specialization.

Reproducibility is insufficient for several central results: the advertised code link is blank, and important details such as prompts and answer extraction, exact domain/reference token lists, preprocessing, training seeds, and full selection procedures are missing. Overall, there may be a useful empirical observation, but the central interpretation and all three headline applications require substantially stronger validation.

strengths: The paper identifies a simple, intuitive connection between contextual-representation geometry and language-model perplexity. The negative correlation is observed across several model families, sizes, layers, context lengths, and text domains.
The layer-wise and training-checkpoint analyses provide useful evidence that the reported geometric pattern emerges through predictive training and becomes stronger in deeper layers.

The authors explore several potential uses of the observation, including model diagnostics, model and layer selection, and an auxiliary training objective. Attempting to test both diagnostic and intervention-based implications is valuable.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and the appendix provides substantial additional plots, hyperparameters, and numerical results.
weaknesses: Several central application claims are not supported by their experiments. Most notably, the kNN-LM section never reports kNN-LM perplexity: it only shows that attention outputs have higher dispersion and relies on prior work for the claim that those outputs perform better. It therefore does not establish that maximum dispersion selects the best retrieval representation.

The purported label-free accuracy predictor is evaluated by using labels to construct artificial mixtures containing prescribed fractions of correct and incorrect examples. This does not demonstrate prospective prediction of accuracy on a naturally occurring unlabeled dataset. Moreover, dispersion is defined for a set of examples, while the paper proposes sorting individual examples by dispersion without defining or validating an individual-level score.

The model-selection evidence is very small and heavily confounded by model family, scale, and specialized fine-tuning. It also changes the method from contextual hidden-state dispersion to a handcrafted sum of distances among selected output-token embeddings. The numerical claims are inconsistent with Table 3: it contains eight rather than nine Qwen checkpoints, and the Euclidean dispersion gap does not perfectly rank them globally—for example, Qwen2.5-1.5B has a larger gap but lower MATH accuracy than Qwen2.5-7B.

Average pairwise cosine distance of normalized vectors is algebraically determined by the norm of their mean vector. Thus, the proposed statistic primarily measures directional centering or anisotropy rather than rich pairwise geometry. The auxiliary objective has the same degeneracy, but this identity and simple competing explanations such as hidden-state norms, mean-vector magnitude, entropy, token frequency, or context difficulty are not analyzed.

The main correlation study bins examples using the same model's perplexity and then computes dispersion within those bins. Although the correlation is broad, the design is observational and vulnerable to difficulty and representation-scale confounds; statistical significance over many dependent bins does not address these confounds.

The training intervention uses GPT-2 Small from scratch, reports only early checkpoints and apparently single runs, tunes the auxiliary weight separately, and provides no uncertainty, equal-compute convergence results, or comparison to standard centering/contrastive regularizers. Consequently, it offers suggestive but insufficient causal evidence.

Given the limited novelty of average cosine dispersion and the substantial gaps between the evidence and the paper's strongest practical claims, the work is not yet competitive for acceptance despite an interesting empirical observation.

strengths: The paper studies a simple, interpretable geometric statistic and presents extensive descriptive evidence across several model families, scales, layers, and text domains.
The progression from observational analysis to potential applications and training interventions is ambitious and clearly motivated.
The appendices include numerous additional plots, held-out-data checks, alternative Vendi-score measurements, hyperparameter details, and a reverse “squeeze” intervention.
The writing and visual presentation are generally clear, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges that the observational results do not establish causality.
weaknesses: The main hardness-ranking claim is not established by the experiment. Dispersion is a set-level pairwise statistic, but the authors first use ground-truth correctness to construct synthetic batches and then measure their dispersion. This shows that artificially selected groups differ; it does not define a score for an individual example or demonstrate that unlabeled examples can actually be ranked or that hard slices can be discovered. The calibration experiment inherits this circular synthetic-batch construction.

The kNN-LM application is unsupported: no kNN-LM datastore, retrieval experiment, interpolation, or resulting perplexity is reported. The paper only shows that attention representations have greater dispersion than feed-forward representations and relies on prior work suggesting that attention keys can perform better. Thus the central claim that maximum dispersion selects the layer with the best kNN-LM perplexity is never tested.

The headline framing conflates within-model sample-level correlations with comparisons of model quality. Most primary plots bin examples from one fixed model by that same model's perplexity; they do not show that models with more dispersed representations are generally better predictors. Dispersion is also not directly comparable across architectures without normalization or controls.

The binning protocol creates groups after sorting by perplexity and then computes correlations across those constructed bins. Reported p-values treat bins as ordinary independent observations and do not address selection, shared examples, lexical/topic/context confounders, or uncertainty across dataset draws. Strong causal explanations about contexts being “pushed” into distinct regions are therefore not warranted.

The model-selection evidence is highly selected and confounded. Specialized Math/Code models are compared with base models using hand-chosen task tokens, but the token lists and reference-token construction are not specified, important baselines such as embedding norms, training step, validation loss, and parameter count are absent, and the OLMo trajectory correlation is confounded by training time. There are also inconsistencies between the stated gap formula and some figure descriptions, and the claimed nine Qwen checkpoints appear to comprise only eight.

The training study is too limited to support a robust improvement claim: GPT-2 Small is evaluated after only 500 and 1000 steps, apparently with one seed, no uncertainty or significance tests, no converged-training results, and no comparison with established contrastive/isotropy regularizers. Auxiliary weights are selected by validation separately, making tuning fairness important but insufficiently documented.

Mathematically, maximizing average pairwise cosine distance among unit vectors is largely equivalent to driving the batch mean toward zero; it does not necessarily yield uniformly informative or discriminative representations and admits degenerate configurations. This issue weakens the proposed geometric interpretation and is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the large appendix: the code footnote has no URL, and key details such as exact prompts, representation token positions, domain-token sets, Python-code data, scoring procedures, and repeated-seed training results are missing. Overall, several advertised applications remain demonstrations of correlation rather than validated methods, which places the paper below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

The paper explores multiple possible uses of dispersion—diagnosis, model screening, representation selection, and training—and includes held-out-data, alternative-metric, and reverse-objective analyses.
The presentation is generally readable, and most figures and tables clearly communicate the reported empirical trends.
weaknesses: The central correlation evidence is methodologically weak. Examples are sorted by perplexity and then aggregated into bins, while dispersion is computed jointly within each bin. Correlating these bin-level quantities can produce strong ecological correlations without showing that dispersion predicts difficulty at the individual-example level. The reported p-values also appear to treat constructed bins as independent observations and do not address dependence induced by pairwise distances.

Average pairwise cosine distance has a simple algebraic dependence on the norm of the mean normalized representation: it is essentially N/(N-1) times one minus the squared norm of that mean. Thus the proposed metric largely measures batch-level mean anisotropy rather than general geometric breadth. This identity, its implications, and comparisons with established isotropy/anisotropy measures are not analyzed, weakening both novelty and interpretation.

The claimed label-free example ranking is not operationally established. Dispersion is a property of a set of examples, not an intrinsic score assigned to one example. The experiments manufacture batches with predetermined mixtures of correct and incorrect examples, demonstrating that group composition changes a group statistic; they do not provide a method or evaluation for sorting individual unlabeled examples or discovering hard slices prospectively.

The calibration experiment is also substantially weaker than claimed: it requires labeled correctness data, constructs synthetic batches at target accuracies, selects among multiple regressors, and reports only aggregate MAE under a fixed model and MMLU distribution. It does not validate transfer to genuinely new domains or naturally occurring slices.

The kNN-LM application never evaluates a kNN-LM. It only observes that final-block attention representations have greater dispersion than feed-forward representations and relies on prior work to imply they would yield better perplexity. Consequently, the headline claim that maximum-dispersion layers identify the best retrieval representations is unsupported; broader layers and actual retrieval/perplexity baselines are required.

The model-selection evidence is small and partly inconsistent with the prose. Comparisons use hand-selected domain-token sets that are insufficiently specified, and Euclidean distances across separately trained models are confounded by embedding norms. The tables contain eight Qwen checkpoints despite the claim of perfectly ranking nine, and the dispersion gap does not reliably order models across parameter scales. There are no comparisons with simple weight-only alternatives such as embedding norms, checkpoint step, model scale, or specialization metadata.

The training evidence is too preliminary to establish a causal or practically meaningful improvement. GPT-2 Small is trained from scratch for only 500–1000 steps, perplexities remain very high, apparently only single runs are reported, and auxiliary weights are selected separately by validation without uncertainty estimates. The squeeze ablation is not causal evidence because adding a strong optimization constraint can degrade training for many reasons. Competitive contrastive/isotropy regularizers and compute-matched baselines are absent.

Several mechanistic claims go beyond the evidence. Greater average distance is equated with clearer distinctions, lower entropy, discriminative features, and embedding-space breadth without testing these mechanisms. The semantic-cluster construction based on sharing a continuation 10-gram does not guarantee semantic similarity, and the stated manual validation is not quantified.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a top-tier paper: the code link is blank, and important details are missing, including exact representation extraction conventions, prompts and scoring for downstream tasks, domain/reference token lists, preprocessing, the Python corpus, generation settings, seeds and variance for training, and complete checkpoint information. Overall, the empirical observation is potentially interesting, but the main practical claims are not sufficiently supported for acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, intuitive geometric statistic and studies it across several model families, scales, layers, and text domains.
The empirical correlation between final-layer dispersion and perplexity is broad and generally consistent; held-out-data and Vendi-score analyses add useful robustness checks.
The appendices provide substantial numerical results, experimental protocols, hyperparameters, and additional analyses.
The training intervention and reverse “squeeze” ablation are promising attempts to move beyond purely observational evidence.
The manuscript is clearly structured, readable, and connects representation geometry to several practically relevant questions.
weaknesses: The central metric has an important unaddressed degeneracy: for normalized vectors, average pairwise cosine distance is determined entirely by the norm of their mean vector (up to a finite-sample factor). Thus it measures alignment to a common direction rather than general geometric breadth, dimensionality, or pairwise structure. The paper neither discusses this identity nor compares against the corresponding centroid/anisotropy baseline.

Dispersion is a set-level statistic, so it cannot directly rank individual examples. The hardness experiments first use ground-truth correctness to construct batches with prescribed accuracy and then measure batch dispersion. This establishes an aggregate association but does not demonstrate the claimed label-free sorting of unseen examples or identification of particular likely errors.

The kNN-LM claim is unsupported by the presented experiment. The paper does not construct a datastore or report kNN-LM perplexity for candidate representations; it only compares dispersion between two sublayers in the final block and relies on prior work for their retrieval performance. This neither validates layer selection nor supports the claim of finding the best representation without search.

The model-selection study uses small, curated collections of related checkpoints and manually selected domain-token sets, with the reference-token construction insufficiently specified. It lacks comparisons to inexpensive baselines such as checkpoint step, model size, embedding norms, validation loss, or output entropy. Euclidean distances are also sensitive to arbitrary embedding scale, and the evidence does not establish robust selection across unrelated candidate models.

Several statistical analyses correlate quantities computed after sorting and binning by perplexity, yet report ordinary Pearson p-values without accounting for bin construction, dependence, or selection. Confidence intervals across independently trained models and tests of predictive generalization across datasets are largely absent.

The causal training evidence is preliminary: GPT-2 Small is trained from scratch for only 1,000 steps, resulting perplexities remain very high, auxiliary weights are validation-selected, and results are reported without multiple-run uncertainty. There are no comparisons against established isotropy or contrastive regularizers, so the intervention's novelty and robustness remain unclear.

Claims such as a “fundamental link,” reliable hard-slice discovery, and a functional causal role for dispersion are substantially stronger than the evidence. The paper supports an interesting empirical association, but multiple headline applications are not actually evaluated end to end.
